meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Writing About Music is Like Dancing About Architecture'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Costello's line. He used it in Musician in 1983 and disowned it in 2008. First close match: Martin Mull, Detroit Free Press, 18 Feb 1979.

answer.label: Not Elvis Costello — Martin Mull said it first
answer.authorDates: 1943–2024 · American comedian, musician, actor and painter
answer.sourceLine: Costello really did say it — in Musician magazine no. 60, October 1983 — but he did not coin it, and in Q magazine’s March 2008 issue he asked to be let off the hook in print and credited Martin Mull instead. The first close match Quote Investigator can document ↗ is a 18 February 1979 “Bob Talbert’s quotebag” column in the Detroit Free Press, which credits Mull. No recording, script or manuscript of Mull actually saying it has ever surfaced, so QI calls him the “leading candidate,” not a proven author.

source.heading: The first time it appears in print
source.excerpt: Martin Mull . . . . . . Comedian-musician on music criticism: “Writing about music is like dancing about architecture.”
trail: 1918–1930 — the ancestor joke. The New Republic of 9 February 1918 carried “Strictly considered, writing about music is as illogical as singing about economics” (H. K. M., “The Unseen World,” Vol. 14, p. 63). Winthrop Parkhurst reshaped it as a simile in The Freeman on 5 October 1921 — “talking about music is like singing about economics” — and repeated it in The Musical Quarterly in July 1930. All three are cited by Quote Investigator ↗; the 1918 issue is digitized at the Internet Archive ↗.

18 February 1979 — the swap to dancing and architecture. “Bob Talbert’s quotebag” in the Detroit Free Press prints the modern wording and credits Martin Mull. Quote Investigator ↗ calls this the first close match and says it is not clear how Talbert heard the line.

Later in 1979 — Mull’s name is already attached. Gary Sperrazza used it in a Sam & Dave profile in Time Barrier Express, September–October 1979: “writing about music is, as Martin Mull put it, like dancing about architecture.” By December 1979 critic Thomas McGonigle was calling it “the famous Martin Mull dictum” in Arts Magazine — though in a painting-swapped form, “Writing about painting is like dancing about architecture.” Wikiquote cites the Sperrazza piece ↗ as the source for its Mull entry.

1983 to 2010 — Costello inherits it, then hands it back. His October 1983 Musician interview was for years the earliest known citation, which is why the line reads as his. In Q, March 2008, he asked to be cleared in print and named Mull. In 2010 blogger Mike Johnston asked Mull’s art dealer Carl P. Hammer to put the question to him, and reported: “Martin confirmed that he is indeed the originator of the famous one-liner.” All documented by Quote Investigator ↗, which notes the confirmation travelled through three people.
source.excerptNote: A quotebag column, so there is no surrounding context — just the credit and the line. Quote Investigator notes the ellipsis dots are in the original. The fuller context comes later, from Costello in Musician, October 1983: “Framing all the great music out there only drags down its immediacy. The songs are lyrics, not speeches, and they’re tunes, not paintings. Writing about music is like dancing about architecture—it’s a really stupid thing to want to do.”

source.rightsNote: Everything documented about this line is modern. Its first known publication is a Detroit Free Press column of 18 February 1979, and the best-known printing is Elvis Costello’s in Musician in October 1983 — both far later than the 1931 US public-domain threshold, so no public-domain claim is available here. The eight-word aphorism itself is short enough that its copyright status as a standalone sentence is untested, and because no original manuscript, script or recording by Mull has ever surfaced, even the underlying authorship is a leading candidacy rather than a settled fact. Quote briefly and with attribution.

author.name: Martin Mull
author.heading: Who was Martin Mull?
author.metaLine: 1943–2024 · American comedian, musician, actor and painter
author.bio: Martin Mull (born 18 August 1943 in Chicago; died 27 June 2024) was an American comedian, singer-songwriter, actor and painter who built a career out of deadpan absurdity — the mock soap Mary Hartman, Mary Hartman, the fake talk show Fernwood 2 Night, Colonel Mustard in Clue, and decades of television work through Roseanne, Sabrina the Teenage Witch and Arrested Development. He was also a serious visual artist, showing paintings that mixed photorealism, pop and collage. The line fits him exactly: a comedian-musician who spent his life in both music and pictures was the ideal person to notice that criticism is a translation between incompatible media — and the earliest print citation anyone has found already had his name on it.

misattribution.heading: Everyone it has been pinned on
misattribution.intro: This may be the most redistributed one-liner in music writing. Quote Investigator ↗ opens its investigation by listing Laurie Anderson, Steve Martin, Frank Zappa, Martin Mull, Elvis Costello, Thelonious Monk, Clara Schumann, Miles Davis and George Carlin as people credited with concocting it. Here is who actually did what.

items.scope: Said it, did not coin it
items.why: He used it in Musician magazine in October 1983 — “Writing about music is like dancing about architecture—it’s a really stupid thing to want to do” — and for years that was the earliest citation anyone had, which is exactly why the line stuck to him. Asked about it in Q magazine’s March 2008 issue he replied: “Oh, God! Can I please put in print that I didn’t say that! I may have quoted it, but I think… Martin Mull coined that. It still follows me around, that one.” Wikiquote files it under Misattributed ↗.

The Los Angeles Times of 18 June 1985 ran the variant “Talking about music is like dancing about architecture” as a subtitle credited to Zappa, in an article by Kenneth Herman. That is six years after the line was already in print credited to Mull, and Quote Investigator ↗ presents no earlier Zappa source.

She flashed the “Talking about music…” variant on the rear projection screen in her 1986 concert film Home of the Brave, which a Philadelphia Daily News review of 18 July 1986 noticed. Asked point-blank on NPR’s Morning Edition on 14 January 2000 whether she had said it first, she answered: “Oh, no, no. It’s one of my absolute favorite quotes” — and credited Steve Martin (transcript excerpt at QI ↗).
Anderson’s 2000 NPR attribution is the best-known source for the Steve Martin version, and it is hearsay. Quote Investigator ↗ documents no citation in which Martin says or writes the line himself.

items.who: Thelonious Monk, Miles Davis, George Carlin, Clara Schumann
items.why: All four appear in the roster of people credited with the saying at the top of the Quote Investigator ↗ investigation, and the article’s chronological run of citations produces no source in which any of them says it. In Schumann’s case the credit is chronologically hopeless: she died in 1896, decades before even the 1918 ‘singing about economics’ precursor.

misattribution.truthLine: The wording that survives — dancing about architecture — first reaches print on 18 February 1979 in “Bob Talbert’s quotebag” in the Detroit Free Press, already credited to Martin Mull, and Mull confirmed authorship through his art dealer in 2010. Quote Investigator’s verdict ↗ is careful and this page follows it exactly: “Martin Mull is the leading candidate for crafter of this maxim.”

context.heading: Why this one refuses to stay attached to anybody
lead: The line is a punchline about a real problem: music is the one art that cannot be paraphrased. A poem or a painting represents something you can describe in ordinary words; a chord progression does not. That complaint is old. The New Republic printed a version of it on 9 February 1918 — “Strictly considered, writing about music is as illogical as singing about economics” — and Winthrop Parkhurst sharpened it into a simile in The Freeman on 5 October 1921 and again in The Musical Quarterly in July 1930, per Quote Investigator ↗.

What changed in 1979 was the imagery. Somebody swapped “singing about economics” for “dancing about architecture,” and the joke became unforgettable — two absurd physical acts instead of one. Because the line reads as something a witty musician would say, it has been redistributed to whichever witty musician the speaker happens to admire: Costello, Frank Zappa, Laurie Anderson, Steve Martin, Thelonious Monk, Miles Davis, George Carlin, even Clara Schumann. Costello, who genuinely did say it once, has spent decades being paid a compliment he keeps trying to return.
context.detailsSummary: The template, and the twist in Mull’s own book
detailsBody: Quote Investigator points out that what really propagates is not a sentence but a template: Writing about music is like ____ about ____, or Talking about music is like ____ about ____. Filled-in variants documented on that page include David Coverdale of Whitesnake (“singing about football,” October 1980), Mike Oldfield (the same, April 1982), John Lennon in his last Playboy interview, and Philip Howard in The Times in August 1991 stacking two at once: “Writing about art is like dancing about architecture or knitting about music.”

There is one honest complication in Mull’s case. In his 1995 book Martin Mull: Paintings, Drawings, and Words, Mull used the line himself — but told it as something he had heard, a story about a painting instructor who told a class that “talking about art is like dancing about architecture.” Quote Investigator notes this may mean he did not originate it, or may simply be a rhetorical distancing device. In 2010 he answered the question the other way: blogger Mike Johnston asked Mull’s art dealer, Carl P. Hammer of the Carl Hammer Gallery in Chicago, to put the question to him, and reported that “Martin confirmed that he is indeed the originator of the famous one-liner.” QI records that this reached print through a chain of three people and says a more direct statement would be desirable. That is why this page says leading candidate and not author.
context.pull: Oh, God! Can I please put in print that I didn’t say that!

schema.verdictNote: Commonly misattributed to Elvis Costello, who genuinely did use the line in Musician magazine in October 1983 but denied coining it in Q magazine in March 2008. Martin Mull is the leading candidate for the coinage, not a proven author: no recording, script or manuscript of him saying it has surfaced, his own 1995 book tells the line as something he heard from a painting instructor, and the 2010 confirmation of his authorship reached print through a chain of three people.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's first close match for 'Writing about music is like dancing about architecture' is the Detroit Free Press, 18 February 1979, 'Bob Talbert's quotebag,' p. 19C col. 5, crediting Martin Mull; QI concludes 'Martin Mull is the leading candidate for crafter of this maxim.'

Elvis Costello used the line in Musician magazine, October 1983 ('Writing about music is like dancing about architecture—it's a really stupid thing to want to do'), and in Q magazine's March 2008 issue denied coining it: 'Oh, God! Can I please put in print that I didn't say that!… I think Martin Mull coined that.'

The 1918/1921/1930 precursors: The New Republic, 9 February 1918 (H. K. M., 'The Unseen World,' Vol. 14, p. 63) — 'writing about music is as illogical as singing about economics'; Winthrop Parkhurst in The Freeman, 5 October 1921; and Parkhurst again in The Musical Quarterly, July 1930.

Other attributions documented by QI: Gary Sperrazza crediting Mull in Time Barrier Express, September–October 1979; Thomas McGonigle's 'famous Martin Mull dictum' in Arts Magazine, December 1979; the Los Angeles Times of 18 June 1985 (Kenneth Herman) crediting Frank Zappa; Laurie Anderson using it in Home of the Brave per the Philadelphia Daily News, 18 July 1986, and crediting Steve Martin on NPR Morning Edition, 14 January 2000.

QI's opening lists Laurie Anderson, Steve Martin, Frank Zappa, Martin Mull, Elvis Costello, Thelonious Monk, Clara Schumann, Miles Davis and George Carlin among those credited with concocting the simile.

In his 1995 book Martin Mull: Paintings, Drawings, and Words (p. 7), Mull told the line as a story about a painting instructor rather than claiming it; in 2010 Mike Johnston reported on The Online Photographer that Mull's art dealer Carl P. Hammer relayed Mull's confirmation that 'he is indeed the originator of the famous one-liner,' which QI notes reached print through a chain of three people.

A dedicated Wikipedia article on the phrase covers the 1918 New Republic precursor, the 1979 Detroit Free Press attribution to Martin Mull, Costello's October 1983 Musician usage and his later denial, and lists the many other people it has been attributed to.

Wikiquote's Elvis Costello page files 'Writing about music is like dancing about architecture — it's a really stupid thing to want to do' under the Misattributed heading, noting Costello denied coining it and tentatively credited Martin Mull.
Wikiquote's Martin Mull page lists 'Writing about music is like dancing about architecture' under Attributed, sourced to Gary Sperrazza's article in Time Barrier Express, September–October 1979.

Martin Mull was born 18 August 1943 in Chicago and died 27 June 2024; he was an American comedian, musician, actor and painter (Mary Hartman Mary Hartman, Fernwood 2 Night, Clue, Roseanne, Sabrina the Teenage Witch, Arrested Development), and the article states that Elvis Costello and Gary Sperrazza attribute the remark to him.
The Internet Archive holds a digitized copy of The New Republic, 1918-02-09, Vol. 14, Iss. 171 — the issue Quote Investigator cites for the 'singing about economics' precursor.
